To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
maternal PJ supplementation in eNOS-deficient mice did not improve uterine artery function or fetal growth, and in fact, reduced fetal abdominal and head size.
PJ supplementation in the eNos−/− mouse does not improve uterine or umbilical artery dysfunction and does not improve fetal growth.
pomegranate juice supplementation alters uteroplacental vascular function and fetal growth in the endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS−/– mouse model of fetal growth retardation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of nitric oxide in the control of uterine artery function in normal pregnancy and pregnancy complicated by fetal growth restriction (fetal growth restriction).
the role of nitric oxide (NO) in the regulation of uterine artery (UtA) function and fetal growth.
the role of maternal vascular dysfunction in the pathogenesis of FGR.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

maternal supplementation with Pomegranate Juice (PJ) during gestation does not improve uterine or umbilical artery (UtA and UmbA) vascular function in either wild type (WT) or eNOS-/- mice and that the changes in UtA and UmbA function are not associated with changes in fetal weight.
PJ supplementation does not improve uterine or umbilical artery vascular function or fetal growth in the mouse model of Fetal Growth restriction.
the PJ supplementation did not improve the uterine and fetal growth outcomes in this mouse model of FGS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PJ has the potential to be a therapeutic agent in FGR, but the data presented in this study do not support this hypothesis.
pomegranate juice supplementation in the mouse model of fetal growth retardation does not improve fetal growth, but rather reduces litter size and fetal biometric measures.
PJ is not beneficial in this mouse model of FGS and that PJ supplementation may actually be detrimental to fetal growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PJ supplementation may not be safe for pregnant mothers.
PJ supplementation has a profound impact on vascular function in both uterine and Umbilical arteries, and these effects are not genotype specific.
maternal PJ supplementation can alter uterine and UmbA function, however these changes do not necessarily translate into improved fetal growth.
